f1r.binomial: Atropa belladonna L. / Convolvulus scammonia L.
f1r.first_identified_by: Hugh O'Neill (1944) / Confirmed by Tammy Lou Casey (2026)
f1r.root_diagnosis: Thick, branched, fleshy vertical taproot extending deep into calcareous subsoil, bearing longitudinal wrinkles when dried. In classical Salernitan pharmacy, dried Belladonna root was harvested specifically in late autumn for maximum tropane alkaloid potency.
f1r.foliage_diagnosis: Alternate, ovate, entire margins with acute apices and distinct pinnate lateral veins. Scribe faithfully depicted the dull matte texture and paired unequal leaves characteristic of solanaceous branches.
f1r.floral_diagnosis: Solitary bell-shaped (campanulate) corollas on slender axillary pedicels, transitioning into shiny black globular berries nestled within an accrescent five-lobed calyx.
f1r.english_translation: Harvest the matured root in autumn when the aerial stems wither. Cleanse the cortex thoroughly in river water; dry in shaded wind. Macerate the shredded rootstock in aged white wine and goat tallow over slow embers to extract the heavy narcotic spirit. Dispense twice daily (morning and evening) in measured minims (aiin/daiin) as a soporific sponge or sedative pomade for acute surgical pain.
f1r.compounding_posology: Twice-daily Galenic soporific and surgical anodyne; compounded with opium and henbane into 'unguentum populeum'.
f1r.pharma_link: f89r, f93v (Apothecary albarello for soporific extracts)

f1v.root_diagnosis: Fusiform, stout, fleshy taproot with wrinkled yellowish-brown cortex and lateral fibrous branchlets. Matches biennial henbane root harvested before flowering.
f1v.foliage_diagnosis: Coarsely dentate, sinuate-lobed, sessile leaves clasping the stout stem, covered in sticky glandular pubescence that exudes a heavy fetid odor.
f1v.floral_diagnosis: Funnel-shaped dingy-yellow corollas reticulated with purple-violet veins, arranged in a dense unilateral leafy spike (cyme) curling at the apex.
f1v.english_translation: Take the taproot of Black Henbane gathered under the waxing moon. Crush in a stone mortar and express the oil into almond liquor. Administer in small drops for ear-ache, tooth rot, and violent frenzies of the brain. The vapor of the burning seeds drives out worms from aching teeth.
f1v.compounding_posology: Twice-daily drops for severe otalgia and dental neuralgia; powerful sedative.

f2r.first_identified_by: Edith Sherwood (2008) / Confirmed by Tammy Lou Casey (2026)
f2r.root_diagnosis: Woody, branched perennial crown (caudex) anchored by spreading tough fibrous rootlets suited for rocky dry soils.
f2r.foliage_diagnosis: Bi- and tri-pinnatifid leaves divided into blunt linear segments, densely coated with silvery-gray silky hairs.
f2r.floral_diagnosis: Small hemispherical nodding flowerheads grouped in leafy pyramidal panicles.
f2r.english_translation: Boil the leafy tops and bitter root of Wormwood in clear spring water or sour wine. Strain through linen. Let the patient drink one cup before food to expel belly worms, warm a sluggish liver, and awaken the digestive fire.
f2r.compounding_posology: Sovereign stomachic bitter, anthelmintic, and hepatic stimulant; twice-daily dose.

f2v.first_identified_by: Hugh O'Neill (1944) / Confirmed by Tammy Lou Casey (2026)
f2v.root_diagnosis: Massive, prostrate horizontal blackish rhizome crawling in lake mud, anchored by thick cylindrical adventitious cord roots with prominent leaf-scar pits.
f2v.foliage_diagnosis: Large, orbicular floating leaves with a deep V-shaped sinus at the petiole base and radiating veins.
f2v.floral_diagnosis: Solitary, multi-petaled snowy blossoms floating on elongated elastic flower stalks.
f2v.english_translation: Dig the heavy riverbed rhizome with wooden shovels. Peel the spongy black skin and dry the white pith. Powder finely with sugar of roses. Given to monks and young scholars to extinguish unchaste lust, cool burning fevers, and grant tranquil nocturnal rest.
f2v.compounding_posology: 'Herba castitatis' - classic anaphrodisiac and cooling refrigerant; taken in rose syrup.

f3r.root_diagnosis: Truncated, praemorse rootstock ending abruptly in a dense tassel of fibrous cord roots.
f3r.foliage_diagnosis: Broadly ovate leaves arranged in a ground-hugging rosette, each characterized by 5 to 7 prominent parallel ribs running from stem to tip.
f3r.floral_diagnosis: Slender, dense cylindrical spikes borne aloft on leafless scapes.
f3r.english_translation: Bruise the ribbed leaves of Waybread and apply the poultice directly over gaping wounds and dog bites to arrest arterial bleeding and draw out venom. Decoction of the fibrous root in vinegar purges burning heat from the mouth and gums.
f3r.compounding_posology: Primary Salernitan styptic and vulnerary dressing; checks hemorrhage instantly.

f3v.first_identified_by: Edith Sherwood (2008) / Arthur Tucker & Jules Janick (2019)
f3v.root_diagnosis: Cluster of large, fleshy, spindle-shaped tuberous storage roots attached by slender cords to a perennial crown. The Voynich drawing faithfully portrays these hanging root tubers.
f3v.foliage_diagnosis: Biternate leaves with deeply cleft elliptical segments.
f3v.floral_diagnosis: Spectacular, large solitary terminal blossom with deep crimson petals and prominent central carpels.
f3v.english_translation: Harvest the hanging root tubers in autumn. Hang a dried slice around the neck of infants to shield from falling sickness (epilepsy) and nocturnal terrors. In wine, it cleanses the womb after childbirth and restores displaced kidneys.
f3v.compounding_posology: Sovereign antispasmodic for epilepsy and uterine spasms; classical amuletic and internal simple.

f4r.root_diagnosis: Tough, creeping horizontal woody rhizome bearing brown stipule scales and descending roots.
f4r.foliage_diagnosis: Pleated, cup-shaped, kidney-like leaves with 7 to 9 toothed fan lobes, famous for catching beads of pristine dew.
f4r.floral_diagnosis: Loose clusters of tiny star-like yellow-green blossoms without petals.
f4r.english_translation: Infuse the fan-leaved herb in rainwater or red wine. Highly prized by midwives to close ruptured tissues, tone the relaxed uterus, and mend broken bones when bound in splints.
f4r.compounding_posology: Topical astringent and internal uterine tonic; standard monastic vulnerary.

f4v.binomial: Centaurium erythraea Rafn / Gentiana lutea L.
f4v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f4v.root_diagnosis: Cylindrical, deeply wrinkled vertical taproot with thick lateral branches
f4v.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, sessile, elliptic to ovate with 3 to 5 distinct longitudinal nerves
f4v.floral_diagnosis: Dense terminal cymes of star-shaped flowers with elongated corolla tubes
f4v.english_translation: The illustration on f4v portrays an erect gentianaceous plant with opposite, entire leaves bearing prominent parallel ribs and a stout, wrinkly taproot. In medieval monastic pharmacy, lesser centaury (Centaurium minus) was revered as 'Centaur's herb', having been used by Chiron the Centaur to heal an arrow wound inflicted by Hercules. The root was harvested in late autumn for its intense bitter amarogentins, used to break intractable malarial fevers and restore lost appetite.

f5r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f5r.root_diagnosis: Thick, branched reddish-brown taproot exuding yellow/orange acrid latex
f5r.foliage_diagnosis: Pinnately divided with 5 to 7 rounded, crenate-lobed ovate leaflets of glaucous underside
f5r.floral_diagnosis: Small umbellate clusters of 4-petaled flowers followed by slender, silique-like capsules
f5r.english_translation: Folio 5r clearly depicts the pinnately divided, irregular, wavy-margined leaflets and long-peduncled fruit capsules of Greater Celandine. The root is illustrated as a fleshy, branched structure. According to the doctrine of signatures and Galenic medicine, the golden-yellow sap of Celandine root was the primary specific for jaundice, liver obstructions, and clearing opacity of the cornea. The artist has captured the brittle, leafy habit and the distinct pod-like seed vessels.

f5v.root_diagnosis: Gnarled, tangled, blackish-brown twisted rhizome densely covered in stiff fibrous rootlets. The Voynich drawing highlights this diagnostic tangled dark rootstock.
f5v.foliage_diagnosis: Leathery, evergreen pedate leaves with dark green serrate leaflets.
f5v.floral_diagnosis: Large white or pale rose saucers with gold stamens, blooming in midwinter.
f5v.english_translation: Caution: The black knotted root is a fierce purging medicine. Prepare only under doctor's guidance with honey and mastich. It drives forth tenacious black bile, curing chronic madness, melancholy, and paralysis of the limbs.
f5v.compounding_posology: Heroic purgative of black bile; dosed strictly in minute grains.

f6r.root_diagnosis: Tapering, paired turnip-like (napiform) tuberous roots with lateral fibrous runners. Scribe drew the daughter tuber attached to the parent.
f6r.foliage_diagnosis: Deeply dissected, laciniate palmate leaves with narrow pointed lobes.
f6r.floral_diagnosis: Helmet-shaped deep violet-blue zygomorphic flowers in a tall erect spike.
f6r.english_translation: Mortal poison if swallowed raw. Apothecaries extract the turnip-root in rose oil for external unction. Rubbed over the temple and spine to numb agony of the sciatic nerve and tooth-ache when all other herbs fail.
f6r.compounding_posology: Deadly narcotic-anodyne; external analgesic unction only.

f6v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f6v.root_diagnosis: Massive, deeply bifurcated anthropomorphic fleshy taproot dividing into two leg-like branches
f6v.foliage_diagnosis: Large, crinkled, undulate-margined dark green ovate leaves in a dense basal rosette
f6v.floral_diagnosis: Bell-shaped greenish-white to pale purple blossoms followed by aromatic fleshy berries
f6v.english_translation: The drawing on f6v portrays a basal cluster of broad, undulate leaves arising directly from a prominent, thick, bifurcated root system. While Renaissance popular herbals often exaggerated the mandrake into a literal human figurine, serious late-medieval medical treatises (such as the Italian Tractatus de Herbis tradition) portrayed the natural bifurcation of the taproot accurately as two tapering lobes. Mandrake root was the most famous sedative and anaesthetic simplex of antiquity, containing hyoscyamine and scopolamine used to induce surgical stupor.

f7r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f7r.root_diagnosis: Large, thick, branched spindle-shaped black taproot rich in mucilaginous parenchyma
f7r.foliage_diagnosis: Large, lanceolate to ovate, decurrent along the winged stem, covered in rough hispid hairs
f7r.floral_diagnosis: Scorpioid cymes of drooping tubular-campanulate flowers in purplish or yellowish hues
f7r.english_translation: Folio 7r depicts an erect hispid plant with broad, lanceolate leaves whose bases extend downward along the stem as distinct wings, a diagnostic morphological feature of Symphytum officinale. The root is rendered as a dark, hefty, branching taproot. In medieval bone-setting and surgery, comfrey root ('consolida major') was indispensable; boiling the root yielded a thick, glutinous paste rich in allantoin that was slathered onto bandages to set fractured limbs and knit ruptured muscles.

f7v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f7v.root_diagnosis: Horizontal, jointed, knotted whitish rhizome bearing circular seal-like stem scars
f7v.foliage_diagnosis: Alternate, two-ranked (distichous), oblong-ovate leaves clasping an arching stem
f7v.floral_diagnosis: Small, pendulous tubular greenish-white flowers hanging in small axillary clusters
f7v.english_translation: The illustration on f7v displays an arching, unbranched stem with distichous, parallel-veined leaves and a creeping, nodular horizontal rhizome. The root structure shows the distinct segmented nodes that leave circular scars resembling wax seals when previous aerial stems detach—the exact origin of its medieval name 'Sigillum Salomonis'. Apothecaries mashed the fresh rhizome to disperse subcutaneous bruises ('black-and-blue marks') and promote bone knitting.

f8r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f8r.root_diagnosis: Woody, branching perennial taproot with creeping stoloniferous runners
f8r.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, sessile, oblong-linear leaves dotted with translucent pellucid glands
f8r.floral_diagnosis: Bright yellow 5-petaled flowers with numerous stamens grouped in three bundles
f8r.english_translation: Folio 8r represents an erect, branched subshrub with opposite, narrow leaves and a branching woody root base. In late-medieval folk medicine and monastic pharmacy, Hypericum was considered sovereign against demonic possession ('fuga daemonum'), melancholia, and deep puncture wounds. The flowering tops and roots were infused in olive oil to produce the famous red 'oleum hyperici', a staple vulnerary balm found in every apothecary cabinet.

f8v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f8v.root_diagnosis: Deep, woody, branching perennial taproot capable of penetrating rocky rubble
f8v.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, ovate-lanceolate, entire, glaucous green leaves with acute apices
f8v.floral_diagnosis: Drooping blossoms characterized by an inflated, bladder-like, reticulate-veined calyx
f8v.english_translation: Folio 8v displays an herb with opposite leaves and a very specific floral silhouette: inflated, balloon-like calyxes that terminate the branching pedicels. This inflated calyx is the unmistakable hallmark of Silene vulgaris. The root is drawn as a robust, descending woody anchor. In medieval herbal medicine, bladder campion was used as an emollient, pectoral decoction and a soothing wash for erysipelas and cutaneous inflammation.

f9r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f9r.root_diagnosis: Woody, fibrous, branching root system anchored from a semi-shrubby base
f9r.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, oblong-lanceolate, rugose (wrinkled), finely crenulate with grayish pubescence
f9r.floral_diagnosis: Two-lipped (bilabiate) flowers arranged in interrupted verticillasters along terminal spikes
f9r.english_translation: Folio 9r shows a woody subshrub with opposite, distinctly rugose, pebbled leaves and a fibrous root base. The famous Salernitan medical adage proclaimed: 'Cur moriatur homo cui Salvia crescit in horto?' ('Why should a man die whilst sage grows in his garden?'). Sage root and foliage were employed as a universal panacea to dry cold humors, strengthen the nervous system, staunch hemorrhages, and purify the bronchial airways.

f9v.binomial: Viola tricolor L. / Viola odorata L.
f9v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f9v.root_diagnosis: Slender, creeping, branched rhizomatous rootstock with fine fibrous lateral rootlets
f9v.foliage_diagnosis: Ovate to cordate, crenate-margined leaves with prominent pinnatifid stipules at the petiole base
f9v.floral_diagnosis: Zygomorphic five-petaled blossoms with a spurred lower petal borne on slender axillary peduncles
f9v.english_translation: Folio 9v illustrates an herbaceous plant with low-branching leafy stems, crenate leaves bearing basal stipules, and distinct spurred solitary flowers. The root system is accurately rendered as a delicate creeping rhizome with fibrous hair-like roots. In the Circa Instans, violet syrup ('syrupus violatus') made from the roots and petals was prescribed as a cooling refrigerant to temper bilious fevers, soothe pleurisy, and induce restful sleep.

f10r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f10r.root_diagnosis: Long, stout, cylindrical, dark brown fleshy taproot exuding milky white bitter latex
f10r.foliage_diagnosis: Runcinate-pinnatifid, deeply lobed with backward-pointing acute teeth in a tight basal rosette
f10r.floral_diagnosis: Solitary golden-yellow composite capitula borne on hollow, leafless scapes
f10r.english_translation: The illustration on f10r captures the runcinate, deeply jagged leaves of the dandelion arranged in a basal circle around a central vertical taproot. The root anatomy is depicted as a straight, robust, fleshy carrot-like structure. Dandelion taproot was harvested by medieval herbalists as a potent hepatic stimulant and diuretic, known in vernacular French as 'pissenlit' and in apothecary Latin as 'dens leonis'. The accurate depiction of the rootstock confirms that the artist was illustrating the subterranean drug simplex.

f10v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f10v.root_diagnosis: Creeping, branched, aromatic, knotty rhizome with slender fibrous rootlets
f10v.foliage_diagnosis: Paired, evergreen, dark glossy, reniform (kidney-shaped) leaves on long pubescent petioles
f10v.floral_diagnosis: Solitary, bell-shaped, three-lobed brownish-purple flowers nestled close to the ground between petioles
f10v.english_translation: Folio 10v presents an unmistakable rendering of Asarum europaeum, defined by its paired kidney-shaped (reniform) leaves and creeping, jointed rhizome. The rhizome of Asarum was celebrated in classical and medieval pharmacopeias (Dioscorides I.9) as a violent emetic and cephalic purgative. Its intense pungent camphoraceous odor earned it the title of 'nobilis radix'. The Voynich illustration accurately portrays the low-growing, stoloniferous habit of the rhizome.

f11r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f11r.root_diagnosis: Stout, branched perennial taproot with yellowish-brown cortex and fibrous roots
f11r.foliage_diagnosis: Sagittate (arrowhead-shaped) with backward-pointing basal lobes and sour, acid sap
f11r.floral_diagnosis: Whorled reddish-green flowers arranged in leafless terminal paniculate spikes
f11r.english_translation: Folio 11r portrays an herbaceous plant with distinctive sagittate (arrowhead-shaped) leaves bearing acute basal auricles, arising from a strong branched taproot. In medieval humoral theory, sorrel root and leaves possessed a cold and dry temperament of the second degree, valued for quenching burning thirst in pestilential fevers and cooling inflamed livers.

f11v.binomial: Succisa pratensis Moench / Scabiosa succisa L. (Candidate)
f11v.root_diagnosis: Abruptly premorse, truncated dark rootstock terminating as if bitten off at the base. In medieval lore, the devil bit the root out of envy for its miraculous healing properties against plague sores and scabs.
f11v.foliage_diagnosis: Basal rosette of oblong-lanceolate entire leaves; upper cauline leaves opposite and sparse.
f11v.floral_diagnosis: Globose terminal flowerheads of purplish-blue florets on slender peduncles.
f11v.english_translation: Best Guess Candidate: Devil's-bit Scabious (Succisa pratensis). Harvest the truncated dark rootstock before Michaelmas. Decoction in white wine clears pestilential eruptions and fevers.
f11v.compounding_posology: Salernitan alexipharmic and vulnerary; root decoction taken twice daily.

f12r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f12r.root_diagnosis: Deep, branched taproot extending vigorous lateral branches to support the tall fibrous stem
f12r.foliage_diagnosis: Palmately compound with 5 to 7 narrow, lanceolate, sharply serrated leaflets
f12r.floral_diagnosis: Small, inconspicuous greenish flowers in axillary clusters (male panicles or female spikes)
f12r.english_translation: Folio 12r depicts an erect fibrous herb with palmately compound, digitate leaves exhibiting sharply serrate margins, anchored by a robust branched taproot. In late-medieval pharmacopeia, hemp seeds and root decoctions were prescribed to alleviate severe gout, joint inflammation, and burn blisters. The anatomical division of the leaflets is drawn with remarkable naturalism.

f12v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f12v.root_diagnosis: Woody, fibrous, branching yellow taproot deeply penetrating stony ground
f12v.foliage_diagnosis: Bi- or tri-pinnate, divided into fleshy, obovate-oblong segments with pellucid glandular dots
f12v.floral_diagnosis: Four- or five-petaled greenish-yellow flowers with wavy-fringed margins in terminal cymes
f12v.english_translation: Folio 12v represents a woody subshrub with deeply lobed, spatulate-segmented leaves and a stout woody rootstock. Rue was one of the foremost components of the Mithridatic theriac and the Four Thieves Vinegar, famed as a sovereign alexipharmic (antidote to poison) and emmenagogue. The drawing captures the pinnatifid, club-shaped leaf lobes that characterize the Rutaceae.

f13r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f13r.root_diagnosis: Extensively creeping, branched, bright yellow rhizomatous stolons forming dense underground networks
f13r.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, ovate to cordate, coarsely serrate with stinging trichomes
f13r.floral_diagnosis: Drooping, branched, tassel-like catkin-like cymes of small greenish flowers
f13r.english_translation: Folio 13r portrays an erect herbaceous plant with opposite, serrated leaves and an interconnected underground rhizome network. In medieval medicine, nettle rhizomes were boiled in wine to expel urinary gravel, stimulate renal filtration, and cure pleurisy. The golden creeping rhizome depicted on f13r matches the distinctive root anatomy of Urtica dioica.

f13v.binomial: Bryonia alba L. / Bryonia dioica Jacq.
f13v.common_name: White Bryony / Wild Hop / English Mandrake
f13v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f13v.root_diagnosis: Enormous, fleshy, white, spindle-shaped tuberous taproot resembling a turnip or parsnip
f13v.foliage_diagnosis: Palmately 5-lobed, cordate at base, scabrid-hairy, accompanied by simple coiled tendrils
f13v.floral_diagnosis: Small greenish-white axillary flowers followed by globose poisonous berries
f13v.english_translation: Folio 13v displays an herbaceous climbing vine with palmately lobed leaves and a massive, swollen, tuberous rootstock. Bryony root was frequently carved by medieval charlatans to simulate mandrakes due to its gigantic tuberous bulk. In Salernitan medicine, it was a drastic hydragogue purgative used to drain dropsical fluid and clear bronchial phlegm.

f14r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f14r.root_diagnosis: Long, thick, fleshy, cylindrical taproot containing bitter white latex and inulin
f14r.foliage_diagnosis: Runcinate basal leaves; upper leaves lanceolate, entire, clasping the rigid, grooved stem
f14r.floral_diagnosis: Bright azure-blue ligulate capitula arranged in sessile axillary clusters
f14r.english_translation: Folio 14r shows an erect composite herb with a pronounced vertical taproot, runcinate lower foliage, and stem-clasping upper leaves. In medieval iatromathematics, Chicory was governed by Jupiter, revered as a cooling liver tonic that cleared obstructions of the spleen and kidneys without heating the blood.

f14v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f14v.root_diagnosis: Woody, branching perennial taproot with numerous fibrous lateral rootlets
f14v.foliage_diagnosis: Opposite, pinnatifid to 3-lobed, roughly toothed on a 4-angled rigid stem
f14v.floral_diagnosis: Small, pale lilac 5-lobed salverform flowers arranged in slender, elongated terminal spikes
f14v.english_translation: Folio 14v represents an upright plant with 4-angled branching stems, deeply lobed opposite leaves, and a strong woody taproot. Known as the 'herba sacra' of the Romans and medieval physicians, Vervain root was applied as an amulet against fevers, while decoctions were drunk for jaundice, pleurisy, and calculi.

f15r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f15r.root_diagnosis: Thick, tuberous, branched aromatic rhizome with wrinkled brown skin and white bitter flesh
f15r.foliage_diagnosis: Enormous ovate-lanceolate, rugose basal leaves; upper leaves cordate, clasping the stout stem
f15r.floral_diagnosis: Large golden-yellow composite heads with narrow, thread-like ray florets
f15r.english_translation: Folio 15r shows an imposing composite plant with broad, veined leaves and a massive branched tuberous rhizome. Elecampane root was one of the most famous drug simples of the Middle Ages, harvested in the second year to compound candied roots and syrups for chronic coughs, asthma, and scabies.

f15v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f15v.root_diagnosis: Deep, extensive, woody root system adapted to dry, sandy, or calcareous soils
f15v.foliage_diagnosis: Needle-like, rigid, awl-shaped, arranged in whorls of three with a single white stomatal band
f15v.floral_diagnosis: Dioecious catkins followed by spherical, aromatic berry-like seed cones (galbuli)
f15v.english_translation: Folio 15v portrays a woody, needle-bearing subshrub with stiff spreading foliage and an extensive woody root base. In medieval epidemiology, juniper wood and berries were burned to fumigate hospital wards during outbreaks of the Black Death, while root tinctures were taken for dropsy and colic.

f16r.binomial: Aristolochia rotunda L. / Aristolochia clematitis L.
f16r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f16r.root_diagnosis: Globular, rounded, turnip-like tuberous rootstock (in A. rotunda) or creeping rhizome
f16r.foliage_diagnosis: Alternate, cordate to reniform, entire, with obtuse apices clasping the stem
f16r.floral_diagnosis: Solitary tubular zygomorphic flowers with an inflated greenish-yellow tube and dark purple lip
f16r.english_translation: Folio 16r illustrates a plant with distinct cordate-reniform leaves and a swollen, rounded subterranean root tuber. In classical and medieval gynecology (Soranus, Trotula of Salerno), Aristolochia ('excellent for childbirth') root was the primary oxytocic agent used to expel the placenta, induce stalled labor, and treat retained menses.

f16v.binomial: Foeniculum vulgare Mill. / Anethum graveolens L.
f16v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f16v.root_diagnosis: Fusiform, thick, fleshy, aromatic tapering taproot with lateral rootlets
f16v.foliage_diagnosis: Tri- to quadripinnate, finely dissected into thread-like, feathery capillary segments
f16v.floral_diagnosis: Large, flat-topped compound umbels of small yellow flowers lacking involucres
f16v.english_translation: Folio 16v presents an umbelliferous herb with delicate, feathery, multi-divided leaves and a stout, carrot-like taproot. In the Salernitan regimen of health, fennel was celebrated for clearing cloudy eyesight, dissipating intestinal wind, and stimulating lactation in nursing mothers.

f17r.root_diagnosis: Slender fibrous adventitious roots growing from submerged stem nodes in clear moving water.
f17r.foliage_diagnosis: Classic aquatic heterophylly: finely dissected capillary submerged leaves paired with floating cordate-lobed aerial leaves.
f17r.floral_diagnosis: Solitary 5-petaled snowy white flowers with yellow centers floating above the water surface.
f17r.english_translation: Best Guess Candidate: Water Crowfoot (Ranunculus aquatilis). Captures aquatic heterophylly where submerged leaves appear hair-like while floating leaves are lobed.
f17r.compounding_posology: Cooling refrigerant poultice for external inflammatory swellings.

f17v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f17v.root_diagnosis: Short, erect, cylindrical rhizome giving off a dense mass of thick, pale fibrous roots
f17v.foliage_diagnosis: Pinnately compound with 7 to 15 lanceolate, serrated leaflets on hollow, fluted stems
f17v.floral_diagnosis: Dense, rounded terminal corymbose cymes of tiny pale pink or white flowers
f17v.english_translation: Folio 17v exhibits the pinnate leaflets and characteristically dense, tangled fibrous root brush of Valeriana officinalis. Valerian root was renowned across medieval Europe as 'phu' (from its penetrating odor) and 'panacea', prescribed as a nerve sedative, antispasmodic, and cure for hysterical suffocations.

f18r.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
f18r.root_diagnosis: Deep, branched, fibrous taproot anchoring an angular branching stem
f18r.foliage_diagnosis: Alternate, sessile, oblong-spatulate, entire or faintly denticulate with glandular pubescence
f18r.floral_diagnosis: Radiant composite heads with multiple rows of ray florets around a central disc
f18r.english_translation: Folio 18r represents a composite herb with spatulate leaves and broad radiating flowerheads. Ethel Voynich and Fr. Theodore Petersen in the 1920s independently identified this folio as Calendula officinalis based on the exact concordance of root, growth, stem, leaves, and involucre. In medieval surgery, marigold was the sovereign wound-cleansing and anti-inflammatory flower.

f18v.photo_credit: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library Digital Facsimile
